metadata.description: 40 new queries (35 positive + 5 negative) covering all 14 newly ingested documents (corpus: 24 sources / 195 chunks). Closes the Phase 5A coverage gap (0/14 new docs had eval queries). Every positive query's evidence_fragments are verbatim substrings verified present in the expected source's chunks in the current vector store.

phase_5a_context.regressions: 18 genuine regressions; 16/18 caused by new-document competition
phase_5a_context.coverage_gap: 0 of 14 new documents had any evaluation queries

design.categories_legacy: existing dataset.json keeps its own categories; proposed set uses directional labels for audit clarity

queries.query: Define 'source' and 'sink' in a directed graph.
queries.expected_evidence: A source is a vertex in a directed graph that has only outgoing edges and no incoming edges. A sink is a vertex in a directed graph that has only incoming edges and no outgoing edges.
evidence_fragments: A source is a vertex in a directed graph that has only outgoing edges and no incoming edges.
A sink is a vertex in a directed graph that has only incoming edges and no outgoing edges.
queries.rationale: Definitions from Module 5-Graph Theory.

queries.query: What is the formal 7-tuple definition of a Turing Machine M?
queries.expected_evidence: A Turing Machine M is a 7-tuple: M = (Q, Σ, Γ', δ, q0, B, F).
evidence_fragments: A Turing Machine M is a 7-tuple, namely.
M = (Q, Σ, Γ', δ, q₀, B, F).
queries.rationale: TM definition from FLAT Module 5. Note glyphs Σ, Γ', δ, q₀ are Unicode subscripted/original as in PDF.
queries.glyph_warning: q₀ uses U+2080 subscript zero; evidence_fragments include the file-exact glyph.

queries.query: How are in-degree and out-degree of a vertex defined in a directed graph?
queries.expected_evidence: In-degree is the number of directed edges that enter at a vertex (deg-(v)); out-degree is the number of directed edges that leave from a vertex (deg+(v)).
evidence_fragments: In-degree of a vertex in a directed graph is the number of directed edges that enter at that vertex.
Out-degree of a vertex in a directed graph is the number of directed edges that leave from that vertex.
queries.rationale: Degree definitions from Graph Theory notes.

queries.query: What does an undefined entry in a Turing Machine transition table mean?
queries.expected_evidence: The undefined entries indicate that there are no-transitions defined or these can be transition to dead state; transition to dead state halts the machine and the input string is rejected.
evidence_fragments: The undefined entries in the table indicate that there are no-transitions defined or these can be transition to dead state.
When there is a transition to the dead state. the machine halts and the input string is rejected by the machine.
queries.rationale: Transition-table semantics from FLAT notes.

queries.query: Compare the Real DOM and the React Virtual DOM: how does each handle updates, and who uses them?
queries.expected_evidence: Real DOM: actual tree structure, directly manipulates on-screen elements (slow for frequent updates), used by all web browsers. Virtual DOM: lightweight in-memory replica using diffing and batching for fast updates, used by libraries/frameworks like React and Vue.js.
evidence_fragments: The actual tree structure of the web page's HTML elements.
A lightweight, in -memory replica of the actual DOM.
Does not directly manipulate the screen; uses diffing and batching for fast updates.
Used by All web browsers (a native web standard).
queries.rationale: Feature comparison table spanning two chunks.
queries.multi_chunk_reason: Intro paragraph (VDOM) and comparison table are in adjacent chunks.

queries.query: Why does PAM run both vector search and BM25, and what does hybrid search add?
queries.expected_evidence: BM25 is exact-match, no model, fast, deterministic; vectors handle meaning, synonyms, paraphrase. Alone either can miss; hybrid fixes both.
evidence_fragments: BM25: exact match, no model needed, fast, deterministic.
Vectors: meaning match, handles synonyms and paraphrase.
Alone, either can miss: BM25 misses "saving notes" for "storing files"; vectors can miss an exact rare identifier like a variable name. Hybrid search (Part 10) fixes both.
queries.rationale: Trade-off rationale Part 9.

queries.query: What are the three system configurations compared in the GPU platform's evaluation strategy?
queries.expected_evidence: Baseline (coding LLM with minimal context), Intermediate (LLM + code-aware RAG), Proposed (LLM + RAG + autonomous execution/feedback loop).
evidence_fragments: Baseline: coding LLM with minimal context.
Intermediate: LLM + code-aware RAG.
Proposed: LLM + RAG + autonomous execution/feedback loop.
queries.rationale: A/B/C experimental design from section 13.

queries.query: Why does the Auto Testing system use both semantic retrieval and BM25, and why RRF for fusion?
queries.expected_evidence: Semantic retrieval handles different wording with same meaning; BM25 handles exact terminology. RRF combines rankings without requiring calibrated scores.
evidence_fragments: Semantic retrieval is strong when the question and source use different wording but have the same meaning.
BM25 is strong when exact words and terminology are important.
Why RRF? It provides a simple way to combine rankings from different retrieval systems without requiring their raw scores to be calibrated to the same scale.
queries.rationale: Why-both rationale present in Auto Testing doc section 6 and section 15 Q&A.

queries.query: In PAM's RRF worked example, which of chunks A, B, C wins, and why?
queries.expected_evidence: B wins (rank 2 + rank 1 beats rank 1 + rank 3), and C loses despite appearing in both lists — depth matters, not just presence.
evidence_fragments: B wins (rank 2 + rank 1 beats rank 1 + rank 3), and C loses despite appearing in both lists — depth matters, not just presence.
queries.rationale: RRF worked example (Part 10); requires understanding of rank fusion.
